clue.text: "Stone walls do not a prison make" (Lovelace). "Yes they do" (Presley)

definitions.text: "Stone walls do not a prison make" (Lovelace). "Yes they do" (Presley)

parts.words: "Stone walls do not a prison make" (Lovelace). "Yes they do" (Presley)
parts.note: Lovelace's poem denies that stone makes a jail; Elvis's 1957 hit names a rocky prison, so the two quotations argue about stone and prisons

explanation.surface: Two quotations debate whether stone walls make a prison, the poet saying no and the rock star yes.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Lovelace's 'To Althea, from Prison' supplies the first line; Elvis Presley's film song names a prison built of rock, turning the poet's metaphor into a pun.
explanation.definitionFit: The Presley song title literally pairs a prison building with stone, the very thing Lovelace dismissed.

clue.text: Director, Frenchman, has knocked guard out cold

parts.note: Jean is a typical French man's first name

indicators.note: knocked about, with out, says the letters of guard and cold are battered into a new order
completes the phrase knocked out, signalling the letters of guard and cold are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A French director has punched a security man unconscious.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram indicator 'knocked ... out' is split round 'guard', and both those letters and 'cold' are rearranged; Jean-Luc Godard was a French New Wave film-maker.
explanation.definitionFit: The New Wave film-maker behind Breathless is a famous French film director.

clue.text: Blairite right to make it snappy

indicators.note: to make it means the letters are made into something else, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A follower of Tony Blair is told to hurry things along by a colleague on the right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make' rearranges BLAIRITE plus R; a Blairite is a supporter of the former British prime minister Tony Blair.
explanation.definitionFit: Snappy describes someone short-tempered, quick to snap at people, as a synonym.

clue.text: Hang around while art is removed from vehicle

indicators.note: removed from says one word is taken out of the vehicle named

parts.note: a hovercraft is a vehicle riding on a cushion of air
craft is a synonym for art or skill

explanation.surface: Someone loiters while artwork is unloaded from a van.
explanation.definitionFit: To hover is to linger or wait about near a place, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Implausible US president found in unworldly setting — word's out

indicators.note: found in says the president is placed within the other letters
a setting surrounds a stone, so the letters of unworldly hold the president
word's out says the letters of word are taken out of unworldly

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, the possessive adding no letter
Ike was the nickname of US president Dwight Eisenhower

explanation.surface: A tale of an American president in a naive, otherworldly place, now that the news is out, seems far-fetched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'word's out' takes W, O, R, D out of the word unworldly, leaving UNLLY; Ike is US president Dwight Eisenhower's nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: Implausible and unlikely are synonyms, both describing something hard to believe.

clue.text: Anticipate demand

definitions.meaning: to anticipate is to look forward to something as likely
to demand is to require something of someone, as in I demand an apology

explanation.definitionFit: Expect means both to foresee an event and to require something of a person as a duty.

clue.text: Perhaps maidens laugh if they go too far

parts.note: a maiden is a cricket over with no runs scored, so maidens are examples of overs
a hoot is a burst of laughter

explanation.surface: Young women laugh when they take things too far.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, an over is a set of six balls and a maiden over is one in which no runs are scored; 'Perhaps' flags maidens as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: To overshoot is to pass beyond a target or stopping point, a synonym of going too far.

clue.text: Spooner's call to girl found among the eucalyptus

indicators.note: naming Spooner says the opening sounds of two words are swapped

parts.note: lo is an old exclamation, a call for attention as in lo and behold
Carla is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A shout to a young woman is heard among the gum trees.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the opening sounds of LO and CARLA, said aloud, gives the sound of the animal's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Koalas live in eucalyptus trees and feed almost only on their leaves, so the phrase describes the animal by its habitat.

clue.text: Doesn't go initially with neural treatment from this guy

definitions.text: Doesn't go initially with neural treatment from this guy

indicators.note: treatment means the letters are worked over and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: initially says only the first letter of go is taken

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A patient who refuses nerve treatment goes instead to this practitioner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treatment' shuffles DOESNT, G (the first letter of go, from 'initially') and NEURAL; the whole clue also describes someone who treats teeth, with nerves often involved.
explanation.definitionFit: A tooth specialist treats nerves in teeth, as in root canals, so the clue as a whole describes the profession.

clue.text: Appearance of girl coming to the centre of Harris

explanation.walkthrough: Harris is an island in the Outer Hebrides of Scotland.

clue.text: Opening words in front of female expert

an ace is an expert

explanation.definitionFit: A preface is the opening text of a book, an introduction to what follows.

clue.text: Latitude to be given to the Queen in future

explanation.surface: The monarch is promised some leeway in time to come.
explanation.definitionFit: Later means at some time afterwards, so it is a synonym of in the future.

clue.text: A flyer for Kay?

parts.note: a flyer is a flying start, and Kay is how the letter K is said, whose start is a kick

explanation.surface: Someone asks what flying machine would suit a woman named Kay.
explanation.walkthrough: A flying start is a fast beginning; Kay spells the letter K, which is the start of the word kick.
explanation.definitionFit: A kick-start is a jolt that gets something going, the same as a flying beginning.

clue.text: Balletic leap is the start of lengthy aerobic manoeuvre

indicators.note: a manoeuvre moves things about, so the letters are rearranged
the start of takes just the first letter of lengthy

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dancer's jump begins a long workout routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'manoeuvre' rearranges L (the start of lengthy) and AEROBIC.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabriole is a ballet jump in which one leg beats against the other in the air.

clue.text: Determined that relative should go under cover

indicators.note: should go says the relative is placed inside the phrase for under cover

parts.note: inside a tent is under cover, giving in tent
sis is short for sister, a relative

explanation.surface: Someone is adamant that a family member should shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: Being in a tent puts you under cover, so the phrase is read as two words, and the relative is put between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Insistent means firmly demanding, so it is a synonym of determined.

clue.text: Genius I'm renouncing, being merely human

taken as written, with the apostrophe adding no letter

explanation.surface: A great talent gives up his own self, revealing himself to be only flesh and blood.
explanation.definitionFit: A mortal is a being who will die, an ordinary human rather than a god.

clue.text: Unoriginal way to measure fractions of a second?

definitions.meaning: second-hand twice removed, received at a further remove from the source

definitions.text: way to measure fractions of a second?
definitions.meaning: after the hour and minute hands, a third pointer on a clock could time parts of a second

explanation.definitionFit: Third-hand information has passed through intermediaries, so it is not original, and a third pointer could tick off fractions.

clue.text: Upset Nurse Pam Kent some time

explanation.walkthrough: Clark Kent is the everyday identity of the comic-book hero, so Kent is him some of the time.
explanation.definitionFit: Clark Kent turns into the caped hero whenever needed, so Kent is the hero for part of the time.

clue.text: Fat bribe

definitions.meaning: fat means a soft oily substance, such as lard
to bribe someone is to pay them off

explanation.definitionFit: Grease is both an oily fat and slang for paying off an official to win favour.

clue.text: Rules that apply when choosing the proper gear?

clue.text: Madonna directed part of "The Pits"

clue.text: Room to grow?
